extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and potential petitioners (attorneys, companies, inventors) considering PTAB post-grant challenges
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on filing and litigating a Post-Grant Review (PGR) petition before the USPTO PTAB under the AIA, including eligibility, timing, grounds, institution standards, costs, estoppel, and strategic considerations. Useful for practitioners evaluating whether to pursue PGR vs other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / scope of PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-grant review (PGR) is an adversarial proceeding before the Patent Trial and Appeals Board (PTAB) of the USPTO, in which a petitioner challenges the patentability of one or more claims in a recently-issued US patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR was created by the America Invents Act (AIA) and became available in 2012; it is designed to challenge recently-issued patents and addresses patentability issues at the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement to file PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR can only be filed within 9 months from the grant of a patent or issuance of a reissue patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 9-month window is strict and often requires advance preparation; missing it makes PGR unavailable (IPR may be an alternative later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a PGR petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person other than the patentee may file a petition for post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petition must identify the real party in interest; practitioners should confirm standing and properly disclose real parties before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted grounds for challenge in PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: PGR allows a third party to challenge the validity of a patent under all statutory grounds for invalidity: Patent ineligible subject matter (§101); Novelty (§102); Obviousness (§103); Written description (§112); Enablement (§112); Indefiniteness (§112); Double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is broader than Inter Partes Review (IPR), which is limited to §102/§103 based on patents/printed publications; include any applicable §101/§112 theories when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard for PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR may be instituted upon a showing that: 'It is more likely than not that at least one claim challenged is unpatentable' OR 'The petition raises a novel or unsettled legal question that is important to other patents or patent applications'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet the 'more likely than not' preponderance threshold or demonstrate the petition presents an important unsettled legal question; institution is the critical gate to full review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline for final determination
rubrics_metrics.description: If instituted, a final determination by the Board issues within 1 year of institution, extendable by 6 months for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect expedited proceedings relative to district court, but schedule can extend for complex cases with good cause shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and typical costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial filing fee: ~$12,000-15,000; Institution fee: ~$18,000-22,000 (if PGR is instituted); Total fees can exceed $30,000-40,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These USPTO fees are only part of the total cost—include attorney fees and possible additional costs; compare costs to IPR and district court litigation when budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effects after final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: After final written decision, petitioner cannot challenge in: civil action (district court litigation), ITC proceeding, or subsequent USPTO proceeding for grounds that were raised OR REASONABLY COULD HAVE BEEN RAISED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR estoppel is broader than IPR estoppel. Carefully evaluate what arguments and grounds are presented or could have been presented to avoid permanently forfeiting later challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic circumstances favoring PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons to choose PGR include: patent contains §101 or §112 issues; desire for broader grounds for challenge; presence of prior art that may not qualify for IPR; within the 9-month window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PGR when substantive issues extend beyond §102/§103 or when early challenge soon after grant is strategically important; prepare quickly due to the 9-month limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic circumstances favoring IPR instead of PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons to choose IPR instead of PGR include: beyond 9-month window (IPR available later); estoppel concerns; lower costs; more established practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh trade-offs—IPR may be preferable when §101/§112 challenges are not needed and cost/estoppel considerations favor IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative features: PGR vs IPR vs Ex Parte Reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Key comparative features include: Timing (<9 months for PGR, after 9 months for IPR, anytime for ex parte reexam); Grounds (PGR: all §101/§102/§103/§112; IPR: §102/§103 only; Ex Parte: §102/§103 only); Prior art considered (PGR: any; IPR/Ex Parte: patents/publications); Discovery (PGR/IPR: limited; Ex Parte: none); Cost (ranges provided); Estoppel (PGR: strong; IPR: moderate; Ex Parte: none); Outcome (final written decision or reexamination certificate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this matrix to choose the appropriate post-grant challenge path based on timing, grounds available, prior art, discovery needs, cost, and estoppel consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical use areas where PGR has been most used
rubrics_metrics.description: PGR has commonly been used for first-to-file applications (post-AIA), software/business method patents, pharma patents with §112 issues, and bringing eligibility (§101) challenges efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical usage patterns when assessing likelihood of success and drafting strategy—certain subject matters see more PGR activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical considerations and drafting/preparation notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical items to account for: the 9-month window is tight and requires preparation in advance; the institution rate is a decision point (gates access to full review); consider parallel district court strategy; evaluate estoppel implications carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan filings and evidence collection early, coordinate parallel litigation strategy if applicable, and draft petitions to maximize institution chances while minimizing estoppel exposure.
